title: End-stage COPD with starting terminal secretions in last days of life
scenario_text: Mrs. Margaret Fernandes, 75, retired from domestic work, lives with her son and daughter-in-law in a small house in Mangaluru. She has end-stage GOLD IV COPD with cor pulmonale, on home O2 24h/day for the past 2 years, has been on Morphine SR 15mg BD plus IR PRN for refractory dyspnea, and was placed on home-based palliative care 4 months ago. She is now in the last days of her life by clinical assessment — bedbound, PPS 20%, drowsy most of the day, taking only sips of fluid, dropping output. The family has accepted that she is dying and wishes for home death (consistent with her stated wishes). Over the last 6 hours, the daughter-in-law has noticed that her breathing has become noisier — a gurgling sound on inspiration and expiration, audible across the room. The patient herself appears peaceful, not in distress, no visible grimacing or struggle, eyes closed, occasional gentle moans on repositioning. Her O2 is on, she is positioned semi-supine. The daughter-in-law is becoming alarmed by the sound, fearing that the patient is 'drowning' or 'choking'. The visiting ASHA worker (who knows the family well) is at the home and rings the helpline for guidance.

patient_demographics.language_spoken: Konkani, Tulu, basic Kannada and Hindi

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: End-stage GOLD IV COPD with cor pulmonale; actively dying
current_medications: Morphine SC 5mg q4h (recently converted from oral)
Hyoscine butylbromide SC 20mg q8h PRN (already in anticipatory kit)

presenting_complaint: Newly noisy 'gurgling' respiration (terminal secretions / death rattle) in an actively dying COPD patient at home; patient peaceful, family alarmed.
asker_query: Madam, aunty's breathing has become very noisy — gurgling sound — for the last few hours. She herself looks peaceful, eyes closed, not in distress. Daughter-in-law is alarmed, thinks she is choking. What to do — give some medicine, suction, position?
ideal_response_components: Reassure the family — this is 'death rattle' (terminal secretions): pooled saliva and bronchial secretions in a dying patient who can no longer swallow or cough; the sound distresses observers but does NOT distress the patient (she is unconscious or near-unconscious — confirmed by her peaceful appearance).

First-line management is POSITIONING — turn her onto her side (lateral or semi-prone, can alternate sides every 1-2 hours); gravity drains secretions and dramatically reduces noise; head slightly down; this often resolves the noise quickly without medication.

Antimuscarinic to reduce NEW secretion production (does not clear existing pooled secretions — give EARLY, ideally at first sign): she already has hyoscine butylbromide PRN in anticipatory kit — give 20mg SC NOW; can repeat q6-8h. Alternatives: glycopyrronium 0.2mg SC q4-6h (preferred — no central effect, less sedation) OR hyoscine hydrobromide 0.4mg SC q4h (crosses BBB, more sedating, may cause paradoxical agitation).

AVOID aggressive oral or pharyngeal suctioning — causes mucosal trauma, patient distress, stimulates more secretion, family upset; gentle oral toilet only with a soft moistened swab to remove any visible secretions at lips and front of mouth.
Reduce or stop any non-essential fluids — SC fluids or any drinks beyond comfort sips add to secretion volume.
Mouth care every 2 hours — moistened cotton swab, water at lips, oral gel (Biotene if available, or coconut oil), lip balm; comfort priority.

Family counselling — this is the most important intervention: explicitly name 'death rattle' to the daughter-in-law; explain in simple Kannada/Tulu/Konkani as she prefers; reassure that the patient is NOT choking or drowning, she is NOT aware of the sound, she is comfortable as evidenced by her peaceful face; the sound is the most upsetting feature for family but not for the patient; explain that this is a sign of the last hours-to-day; offer to sit with the family for a few minutes.

Anticipatory communication: this is a sign of the last 24-48 hours; reinforce that family preference for home death is being honoured; check whether all immediate family is present or wants to be called; ask about last-rites preferences (Konkani Christian family — likely Catholic — last rites/anointing of the sick, family prayer; if Hindu — tulsi water at lips, mantras); facilitate.

Continue O2 (comfort), morphine for any pain/dyspnea signs (her current 5mg SC q4h is appropriate); add midazolam 2.5mg SC PRN only if there is true distress (facial grimacing, restlessness, accessory muscle use) — not for the noise alone.

Plan: home palliative team telephone follow-up; expect death within hours to a day; ensure family knows what to do at the time of death (signs, who to call, immediate practical steps — death certificate from family physician or palliative team).
expected_guideline_citations: EAPC Recommendations on Death Rattle (Wee 2008; updated 2017)
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care (2nd ed.) — Terminal secretions; Last 48 hours
NICE NG31 — Care of dying adults in the last days of life
Cochrane Review on Antimuscarinic Drugs for Death Rattle (Wee 2008)
safety_traps: Aggressive suctioning — causes trauma and stimulates more secretions; major source of patient distress at end of life.
Delaying antimuscarinic until secretions are heavy (existing secretions do not respond — start at first sign).
Adding SC fluids 'to keep her hydrated' — adds to secretion volume.
Sedating the patient with midazolam solely for the family's distress at the sound.
Failing to reassure the family — they interpret the sound as suffocation; this is the highest-impact intervention.
Sending the patient to hospital at this stage — against goals.
indian_context_notes: Konkani-Tulu Catholic family in coastal Karnataka — religious last rites (anointing of the sick by a Catholic priest); family may wish to call the parish priest.
Mangaluru has strong palliative care infrastructure (Father Muller Hospital palliative unit, FMMC, KMC Manipal nearby).
Home death in coastal Karnataka is increasingly accepted as the preferred mode for elderly with chronic disease.
Kannada/Tulu/Konkani register — use plain, gentle language with the ASHA who will translate; avoid clinical terms like 'death rattle' (translate as 'antya samay shabd' or 'maranatik dhwani').
Hyoscine butylbromide is on NLEM and affordable; glycopyrronium less widely stocked in rural India.
ASHA in long-term village relationship — can support family through the dying hours and the immediate post-death period.
